w:r.w:t: This document captures the full design discussion for a web application that combines a research paper reading environment with a structured knowledge management system (LLM Wiki). The system is designed to support the entire research workflow: from discovering and reading papers, through extracting and organising knowledge, to forming original ideas and planning experiments.
Core goal: reduce the friction between reading a paper and acting on it — whether that means understanding it, coding from it, or building a novel idea on top of it.
User specifies a subject → system crawls and surfaces relevant papers
Clicking a paper opens a full reading view
Paywalled papers show an upload prompt so users can provide their own PDF
A sidebar accompanies every paper with two modes:
General chat: ask questions about the paper at large
Selection chat: highlight any text passage, then ask about that specific excerpt
Whenever text is highlighted, the system surfaces two options simultaneously:
"Ask in Chat" — opens the selection in the sidebar chat without saving
"Save to Wiki" — opens a lightweight form (Type, Research, Quick note) and stores the excerpt as a typed node in the wiki
The source paper, section reference, and raw highlight text are captured automatically — the user only needs to classify and annotate.

A dedicated panel ("My Work") sits alongside the reading view with three tabs: Questions, Ideas, and Experiments. This is where the user creates and manages their own research contributions, linked back to the nodes collected from papers.

_shared/ prevents duplication: a method like BM25 or a concept like 'attention mechanism' that appears in five different research projects is stored once and linked to many. _graph.json tracks all cross-research edges.
The wiki defines seven node types. Each node carries a source reference (paper, authors, year, section, raw highlight) so every piece of knowledge is traceable back to where it came from.
Techniques that can be adapted or implemented
Your own ideas synthesised from nodes
3.3 Lineage — Why It Matters for Coding

The most important design principle is that every YourIdea and Experiment records its full lineage: which methods were adapted, which concepts informed it, which results serve as baselines. When a user sits down to implement, they can follow the graph:
├── adapted from method_003 (MaxSim Scoring, ColBERT v2 §3.2)
│ algorithm_sketch: for each q, score += max(sim(q, d_i))
│ adapt_notes: 'replace MaxSim with learnable soft attention'
└── baseline: result_007 (ColBERT v2, F1=87.3 on HotpotQA)
Everything needed to write the code is already in the graph — no need to re-open the original paper.

The lightest-weight path. When the user highlights text in a paper, a small popup appears with exactly three fields: node type, target research, and an optional quick note. Everything else (source, section, highlight text) is auto-populated from context. The user can also choose 'Ask in Chat instead' to route the selection to the sidebar without saving.
The user opens the Ideas tab and clicks New Idea. The form has a title field, a free-text contribution field (markdown supported), a status selector, and the critical 'Built from' section.
Solving the 'too many nodes' problem in Built From
Showing a flat list of all nodes becomes unusable once the wiki has 50+ entries. The solution uses three layers:

Layer 1 — Auto-suggest: as the user types the idea title and contribution, the system analyses the text and surfaces the most semantically relevant nodes as one-click suggestions. No searching required for the common case.
Layer 2 — Search: a search box with type-filter buttons (Method, Insight, Concept, Result) lets the user find anything by keyword across title, notes, and paper name.
Layer 3 — Browse: a research + subject scope filter narrows the list when the user knows roughly where to look.

Tags added via any layer appear as dismissible chips in the Built From area. This is the step where lineage is created — so reducing friction here is the single most important UX decision in the whole system.
Entry Point 3 — New Experiment (from a YourIdea)
Triggered by clicking 'Run Experiment' on any idea. The form pre-fills the idea reference and auto-suggests baselines and methods from that idea's lineage. The user only needs to confirm or adjust.

Methods that already have status 'done' are displayed dimmed and unchecked by default. They remain visible so the user understands the full context, but they do not clutter the selection. Methods with status 'to-implement' are checked by default.
After running the experiment externally, the user returns to log results: one row per metric (name + value), a notes field, and a status update. The delta vs baseline is computed automatically.
Because nodes are linked, a naive delete can silently break the knowledge graph. The system uses dependency-aware deletion:
Warn → offer Archive (hide from view, keep in graph) or hard delete + remove links
Warn → delete idea + unlink dependent experiments
Confirm dialog → delete with logged results
For source nodes (Concept, Method, Result, Insight) that have dependents, the recommended action is Archive rather than delete. An archived node is:
Hidden from all suggestion lists and browse views
Still present in _graph.json so existing idea and experiment lineage stays intact
Recoverable — the user can unarchive at any time
A hard delete with 'Remove links' is available but always requires explicit confirmation. The goal is that a user can never accidentally destroy lineage silently.

Too many nodes to choose from
Auto-suggest from text currently being typed
Full-text search by title, paper name, and notes
Browse filter scoped to research + subject
Methods already implemented appear as options
Dimmed + unchecked by default in Experiment Builder
Dependency warning before any destructive action
Soft delete (archive) for source nodes; hard delete only after explicit confirmation
Schema design for _graph.json and the query patterns it needs to support (e.g. 'all unimplemented methods linked to active ideas')
Interactive prototype of the full layout: paper view + sidebar chat + workspace panel
Auto-suggest engine: embedding-based similarity vs keyword matching vs LLM classification
Conflict resolution in _shared/ when two researches modify the same node
Export formats: can the wiki export a structured literature review or experiment log automatically?

The prototype phase should prioritise Entry Point 2 (New Idea + Built From) — this is the highest-friction step and the one most likely to determine whether users build genuine lineage or treat the wiki as a flat note dump.
